markdown.headingText: The design rule that makes these work
markdown.markdown:
Five crowd games: **Catch or No Catch?**, **Out or Safe?**, **Guess the Gun**,
**How Far Did It Go?**, and **Beat the Burner**.

::: {.callout-important}

A question is only worth asking when the answer is genuinely uncertain. A prompt
the crowd gets right 95 % of the time is a formality, not a game.

So every selector below ranks candidate plays by **suspense**, not by size. The
most spectacular catch of the night is usually a *bad* vote — everyone can see
it was caught. The best vote is the one the model itself is unsure about.
:::

We define suspense directly from the model's own uncertainty:

$$\text{suspense} = 1 - \left|\,2\left(P - 0.5\right)\right|$$

which peaks at $P = 0.5$ and falls to zero at either certainty.

## Catch or No Catch?

Freeze at contact, take the vote, then reveal the model's odds and the outcome.
Only fly balls with catch probability between 0.25 and 0.75 qualify.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-catchvote
#| eval: false
source("../R/R08_fan_interactive.R")
catch_or_no_catch(scored, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-catchvote
#| eval: false
from components import c08_fan_interactive as c08
scored = model.score_frame(tabs["catches"])
c08.catch_or_no_catch(scored, top=10)
```

:::

Each row carries the prompt, the two options, the model's answer, and the truth
— everything a control room needs to run the segment.

## Out or Safe?

A bang-bang play at first. The close-play calculator compares when the throw
would arrive against when the runner did:

$$\text{margin} = t_{\text{ball arrives}} - t_{\text{runner arrives}}$$

Plays inside ±0.15 s are flagged `bang_bang` and are the only ones offered to
the crowd.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-safevote
#| eval: false
out_or_safe(close_plays, max_margin_s = 0.15, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-safevote
#| eval: false
c08.out_or_safe(close_plays, top=10)
```

:::

Ball arrival is derived from the measured throw velocity and the distance from
the fielder to the bag; runner arrival is the frame he enters the bag radius.
Both come from tracking, so the replay confirms the verdict.

## Guess the Gun

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-gun
#| eval: false
guess_the_gun(pitches, min_velo = 90, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-gun
#| eval: false
c08.guess_the_gun(tabs["pitches"], top=10)
```

:::

Options are generated as three 3-mph buckets straddling the true reading, so the
guess is meaningfully hard but never unfair.

## How Far Did It Go?

Same idea in 25-foot buckets, offered on balls that carried at least 330 ft.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-far
#| eval: false
how_far_did_it_go(hits, min_distance = 330, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-far
#| eval: false
c08.how_far_did_it_go(tabs["hits"], top=10)
```

:::

## Beat the Burner

A fan taps their phone; the app races that reaction against a real runner. The
target is how long the runner needed to cover 90 feet at his peak speed.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-beat
#| eval: false
beat_the_burner(sprints, baselines, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-beat
#| eval: false
c08.beat_the_burner(tabs["sprints"], baselines, top=10)
```

:::

Each target carries its league percentile, so the crowd knows whether they are
chasing an average runner or the fastest man in the league.

## The night's slate

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-slate
#| eval: false
game_night_slate(catch_df, gun_df, far_df, burner_df, safe_df)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-slate
#| eval: false
c08.game_night_slate(catch_df, gun_df, far_df, burner_df, safe_df)
```

:::

In the showcase game the engine found **33 plays** that qualified as genuine
fan-vote moments — roughly one every half-inning, which is about the right
cadence for in-game entertainment.
